{"id": "39:36/q17", "question": "What inward demand follows from God's sufficiency?", "turns_on": "Exclusive reliance, self-purification, or contemplation of God's care.", "positions": [{"id": "39:36/q17/p1", "position": "Seek sufficiency from God alone, not hope or fear from creatures.", "reasons": "Abu Bakr ibn Tahir says discontent with divine sufficiency means ruin; Ibn Ata says hoping in, fearing or coveting creatures forfeits servitude. {"id": "39:36/q18", "question": "What Prophetic teachings illustrate sufficiency and reliance?", "turns_on": "The reports give different practical forms of sufficiency.", "positions": [{"id": "39:36/q18/p1", "position": "Rely on God alone; people cannot benefit or harm beyond His decree.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas transmits counsel to obey God, ask and seek help only from Him; patience brings relief and ease follows hardship."}, {"id": "39:36/q18/p2", "position": "Success joins guidance to Islam, sufficient livelihood and contentment.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports the saying; al-Tirmidhi graded it sahih."}, {"id": "39:36/q18/p3", "position": "Purified religion makes a little deed sufficient.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports the Prophet's advice to Muadh."}, {"id": "39:36/q18/p4", "position": "God suffices the worldly and afterlife concerns of one who wakes with a single concern.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this hadith."}]}
{"id": "39:36/q19", "question": "What figurative examples clarify compressed and extended likenesses?", "turns_on": "Whether the intended comparison is immediately apparent or requires explanation.", "positions": [{"id": "39:36/q19/p1", "position": "A familiar simple likeness can be compressed into metaphor.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani illustrates with a brave man called a lion and a beautiful woman called the sun."}, {"id": "39:36/q19/p2", "position": "A complex likeness needs explanatory clauses rather than a compressed metaphor.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani says calling a man 'night' alone suggests darkness or misses that a fugitive cannot escape his reach."}]}

{"id": "39:50/q14", "question": "What does the attached literary discussion say about Qur'anic order and comparison with poetry?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:50/q14/p1", "position": "The Qur'anic discourse compresses many lessons into a few verses and maintains a connected order across changing topics.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī says a longer account would be needed otherwise; he traces warning, return of deeds, and hope of mercy with 17:7–8, and says unrelated insertion would disrupt the order while continued study yields further wisdom."}, {"id": "39:50/q14/p2", "position": "Comparison with Imruʾ al-Qays's poetry fails because some poetic diction and lines are obscure, coarse, or inept.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī rejects the comparison; he reports al-Aṣmaʿī could not explain san, sannaq, and sanam, while another gloss makes sannaq a hill."}]}
{"id": "39:50/q15", "question": "What rhetorical images and relations are discussed in the attached poetry notes?", "turns_on": "These are separate poetic examples, with no dispute among the notes.", "positions": [{"id": "39:50/q15/p1", "position": "The dawn slapping a horse's brow and being avenged in its belly is the more skillfully compact image.", "reasons": "Jurjānī compares it favorably with a preceding poetic example."}, {"id": "39:50/q15/p2", "position": "A chain image extends the familiar likeness of water ripples to armor rings.", "reasons": "Jurjānī says the current is then imagined carrying chains."}, {"id": "39:50/q15/p3", "position": "An image linking speed to madness and slowness to reason works through familiar associations.", "reasons": "Jurjānī ties extreme speed to madness and deliberate pace to reason."}, {"id": "39:50/q15/p4", "position": "A trembling sword is imagined as afraid of the warrior, perhaps borrowed by Ibn Bābak from Ibn al-Muʿtazz.", "reasons": "Jurjānī reports Ibn al-Muʿtazz's invented cause for a sword's shaking and conjectures that Ibn Bābak borrowed it."}]}

{"id": "39:50/q19", "question": "How do the attached notes classify Qur'anic content and word sciences?", "turns_on": "The lists differ in how finely they divide Qur'anic content and language sciences.", "positions": [{"id": "39:50/q19/p1", "position": "Qur'anic content can be grouped as command, prohibition, report, and question, with other lists adding Sunna, promise, and threat.", "reasons": "Burhān reports these alternative short classifications."}, {"id": "39:50/q19/p2", "position": "Thirty kinds of content may be enumerated, including warning, Paradise and Hell, divine attributes and favors, arguments, contrasts, wisdom, praise, and blame.", "reasons": "Burhān transmits ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā's list."}, {"id": "39:50/q19/p3", "position": "Al-Ṭabarī's three broad categories encompass the thirty and more, while Qur'anic wonders remain inexhaustible.", "reasons": "Abū al-Maʿālī prefers this, citing the verse on God's keys of the unseen, 6:59."}, {"id": "39:50/q19/p4", "position": "Four sciences of Qur'anic words are iʿrāb, naẓm, morphology, and iʿtibār; the last gauges the first three and permits inference.", "reasons": "Burhān reports this classification and illustrates morphology through aqsaṭa/qasaṭa (justice/injustice) and two forms of baʿuda (distance/perishing)."}]}

Tabataba'i says the seven gates open for entry."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q07", "question": "What are the seven gates or levels called and ordered?", "turns_on": "The reports reverse the order of the named levels.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q07/p1", "position": "From lowest upward: Jahannam, Lahza, Hutama, Saqar, Jahim, Sa'ir, Hāwiya.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i reports this from Ali, describing seven stacked gates or levels."}, {"id": "39:71/q07/p2", "position": "Hāwiya is lowest and Jahannam highest.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i reports this reversed order from al-Kalbi."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q08", "question": "What do Hell's seven gates signify inwardly?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q08/p1", "position": "They signify seven blameworthy traits through which entrants pass.", "reasons": "Bursevi lists pride, stinginess, greed, lust, envy, anger and rancor; the soul should be purified of them."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q09", "question": "How does the construction with ḥattā and idhā work?", "turns_on": "Whether the expressed opening completes the conditional directly or an implied repeated arrival does.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q09/p1", "position": "The answer to idhā is 'its gates were opened'.", "reasons": "Nahhas contrasts Paradise's omitted answer. Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan say the explicit answer makes arrival the condition of opening; Baydawi says ḥattā introduces and depicts the following sentence. Bursevi calls it a narrative clause; Ibn Ashur calls ḥattā a new start and idhā a future time adverb with conditional force; Samarra'i says omitting mā presents an ordinary arrival-opening sequence, unlike 41:20."}, {"id": "39:71/q09/p2", "position": "The full implied construction repeats 'they arrived' before the doors opened.", "reasons": "Burhan says ḥattā requires completion, so an implied repetition of jāʾūhā completes it."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q10", "question": "How is futiḥat read, and what does the form suggest?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is geminated to mark repeated or emphatic action, or light for a single opening.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q10/p1", "position": "The tāʾ is doubled, conveying repeated, abundant or intensified opening.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid and Ibn al-Jawzi name Ibn Kathir, Nafiʿ, Abu ʿAmr and Ibn ʿAmir; Ibn Atiyya calls this the majority. Ibn Khalawayh says each door's opening may recur and cites 12:23 and 38:50; Thalabi and Baghawi describe repeated or abundant action. Qiraat-ER allows multiple gate access or emphatic opening. Nashr says the readers other than the Kufans double the tāʾ in both occurrences of futiḥat in this sura and at its occurrence in al-Naba."}, {"id": "39:71/q10/p2", "position": "The tāʾ is light, describing a single opening.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujahid and Ibn al-Jawzi name Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i; Ibn Atiyya also lists Talha and al-Aʿmash. Thalabi, Baghawi, Baydawi and Nasafi call it the Kufan reading. Ibn Khalawayh prefers it because this action is not repeated. Nashr says the Kufan readers lighten the tāʾ in both occurrences of futiḥat in this sura and at its occurrence in al-Naba."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q11", "question": "Why is there no waw before Hell's gate opening, unlike Paradise's?", "turns_on": "The grammatical force of waw and whether the gates stand open before arrival.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q11/p1", "position": "Hell's arrival triggers opening; Paradise's gates are already open.", "reasons": "Nahhas reports the Basran view that waw is meaningful coordination, unlike the Kufan claim that it is extra. Ibn Atiyya compares open homes ready for joyful visitors. Abu Ali rejects the waw-of-eight account, taking Paradise's waw as circumstantial. Samarra'i compares open Paradise with a closed prison and cites 38:50."}, {"id": "39:71/q11/p2", "position": "The Paradise waw is extra and the answer is its gates opening.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports the construction joining arrival and opening; Nahhas assigns the extra-waw account to Kufans and says Basrans reject it."}, {"id": "39:71/q11/p3", "position": "Paradise has eight gates, Hell seven; the waw is a waw of eight.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this proposed explanation. Abu Ali explicitly rejects it."}, {"id": "39:71/q11/p4", "position": "Paradise's answer is omitted because its blessings exceed expression.", "reasons": "Nahhas states the Paradise answer is omitted. Samarra'i says language cannot encompass the blessings and the answer lies within Paradise."}, {"id": "39:71/q11/p5", "position": "The Paradise waw can coordinate an appositional expression.", "reasons": "Jishumi adduces 21:48, where Moses and Aaron's Criterion and light exemplify conjunction understood as apposition."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q12", "question": "Who are Hell's keepers?", "turns_on": "Literal angelic custodians and Qashani's symbolic account.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q12/p1", "position": "They are angels appointed to guard and punish Hell's people.", "reasons": "Nasafi and Bursevi specify their punitive charge; Ibn Kathir calls them the harsh and powerful Zabāniya. Qurtubi gives khāzin as the singular of khazana, like sādin and sadana. Study Quran says there are nineteen, citing 74:30; Tabataba'i calls them angels."}, {"id": "39:71/q12/p2", "position": "Inwardly, Mālik and the Zabāniya symbolize bodily nature and the earthly angelic realm.", "reasons": "Qashani says that realm is assigned to lower selves."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q13", "question": "What is the point of the keepers' question?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q13/p1", "position": "It rebukes and humiliates the condemned for rejecting a warning they received.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Baghawi, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Biqa'i, Alusi and Islahi call it reproach; Biqa'i says it compounds punishment. Jishumi says it shows their acts came from themselves. Study Quran cites parallel rebukes at 40:50 and 67:8–9. Kuranyolu says it also warns living readers while change remains possible."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q14", "question": "How is 'did messengers come to you' read?", "turns_on": "The gender agreement of the verb with messengers.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q14/p1", "position": "The verb has masculine yāʾ: yaʾtikum.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls this the majority; Abu Hayyan likewise contrasts it with a feminine reading."}, {"id": "39:71/q14/p2", "position": "The verb has feminine tāʾ: taʾtikum.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya names al-Aʿraj; Abu Hayyan, Samin and Alusi name Ibn Hurmuz."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q15", "question": "Who are the messengers 'from among you'?", "turns_on": "Whether 'from among you' stresses common humanity or the same community.", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q15/p1", "position": "They are human messengers from the condemned people's own kind or peoples.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls them from among the people. Ibn Atiyya, Ibn Kathir, Abu Hayyan, Biqa'i, Bursevi and Alusi say shared speech, access and understanding strengthened the proof. Tabataba'i explicitly says human messengers; Nasafi calls them children of Adam."}, {"id": "39:71/q15/p2", "position": "The messengers are specifically from the unbelievers' own communities.", "reasons": "Tabari phrases the question as messengers from among the disbelievers and sent to their peoples; Muqatil says from among the people addressed."}]}
{"id": "39:71/q16", "question": "How does minkum attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:71/q16/p1", "position": "It may qualify 'messengers' or attach to the action of coming.", "reasons": "Samin gives both analyses."}]}
